```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5.5,
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 96,
  fig.retina = 1
)
```

Drug overdose deaths among white men in the United States increased steeply
after 2000, but the role of birth cohort is less clear. This vignette
reproduces Figure 1C/D of Jalal and Burke (2020) and looks at the same data
in a few other ways.

```{r setup}
library(hexamap)
```

## The data

`overdose_white_men` has accidental drug overdose death rates (underlying
cause ICD-10 X40-X44) per 100,000 white men by single year of age (15-70)
and calendar year (1999-2018), from CDC WONDER.
`overdose_white_men_long` has the same data with deaths, population and a
reliability flag:

```{r data}
head(overdose_white_men_long)
table(overdose_white_men_long$flag)
```

CDC WONDER considers rates based on fewer than 20 deaths unreliable, and its
data use restrictions do not allow publishing counts of 9 or fewer deaths.
The 63 rates based on 10 to 19 deaths were computed from the deaths and
population; the 20 cells with 9 or fewer deaths are `NA`, and are shown in
grey below. They are at ages 15-16 and, before 2006, at ages 61-70.

## Lexis diagram and hexamap

The paper's Figure 1C/D, with the same color limits (0 to 40 deaths per
100,000) and the paper's jet palette:

```{r figure-1, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of drug overdose death rates among white men, ages 15 to 70, 1999 to 2018. Rates rise sharply after 2015, mainly between ages 25 and 55, and are low below age 18."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
lexis_map(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40), legend = FALSE,
          title_text = "C. Lexis diagram")
hexamap(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40),
        scale_units = "Deaths per\n100,000", na_label = "Suppressed",
        title_text = "D. Hexamap")
```

Both show the period pattern (the rise since 2015) and the age pattern (low
rates below age 18). The cohort pattern is easier to follow on the hexamap.

## Following a cohort

The paper compares the men born in 1975 with men aged 25. Both lines span
exactly 20 years, from 1999 to 2018:

```{r cohort-1975, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap with the 1975 birth cohort and age 25 highlighted in white. On the Lexis diagram the cohort line is longer and drawn at 45 degrees; on the hexamap both lines have the same length."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
highlight <- list(cohort = 1975, age = 25, col = "white", lwd = 2)
lexis_map(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40), legend = FALSE,
          highlight = highlight, title_text = "Lexis diagram")
hexamap(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40), legend = FALSE,
        highlight = highlight, title_text = "Hexamap")
```

On the Lexis diagram the 1975 cohort line is about 41% longer than the
age-25 line, so the cohort's increase seems slower than the increase at age
25. On the hexamap the two lines have the same length, which shows that the
two increases are similar.

The rates along the two lines:

```{r cohort-table}
d <- overdose_white_men_long
cohort_1975 <- d[d$year - d$age == 1975, c("year", "age", "rate")]
age_25 <- d[d$age == 25, c("year", "age", "rate")]
merge(cohort_1975, age_25, by = "year", suffixes = c("_cohort_1975", "_age_25"))
```

## Relative change

A rate ratio relative to a reference year removes the age pattern and leaves
the changes over time. With a log scale and `midpoint = 1`, increases and
decreases of the same size get colors of the same strength:

```{r ratio, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Hexamap of rate ratios relative to 2005 on a diverging log scale. Ratios rise above 1 after 2005 at most ages, most strongly among men in their sixties, and fall below 1 for teenagers."}
ratio <- overdose_white_men / overdose_white_men[, "2005"]
hexamap(ratio, colorbar_scale = "log", midpoint = 1,
        scale_units = "Rate ratio\nvs 2005", na_label = "Suppressed",
        highlight = list(cohort = 1975, col = "black"))
```

By 2018, rates at most ages were 2 to 3 times their 2005 level, and 5 to 9
times among men in their sixties, while they fell for teenagers:

```{r ratio-2018}
round(summary(ratio[, "2018"]), 2)
round(ratio[c("17", "30", "45", "65"), "2018"], 1)
```

## Spreading the colors

The highest rates (above 60 per 100,000) are much higher than most. A
quantile scale gives each color the same number of cells, which shows
differences among the lower rates:

```{r quantile, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Hexamap of the overdose rates on a quantile color scale, with percentiles on the left of the colorbar and rates on the right."}
hexamap(overdose_white_men, colorbar_scale = "quantile",
        scale_units = "Deaths per 100,000", na_label = "Suppressed")
```

## Reference

Jalal H, Burke DS. Hexamaps for age-period-cohort data visualization and
implementation in R. *Epidemiology*. 2020;31(6):e47-e49.
<https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001236>

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Health
Statistics. Multiple Cause of Death 1999-2018 on CDC WONDER Online Database.
<https://wonder.cdc.gov/mcd-icd10.html>
